questions.question: Which best describes "DataFrame to SQL" as taught in the lecture?
options: It allows a pandas DataFrame to be written into a database table using the DataFrame.to_sql method, optionally appending to an existing table.
It converts a SQL query result directly into a DataFrame without needing pandas.
It requires creating a new database engine for each DataFrame insertion.
It can only read from a database, not write to it.
questions.distractor_a: It can only read from a database, not write to it.
questions.distractor_b: It converts a SQL query result directly into a DataFrame without needing pandas.
questions.distractor_c: It requires creating a new database engine for each DataFrame insertion.

questions.question: Which best describes 'GROUP BY' as taught in the lecture?
options: It groups rows by specified columns and then applies aggregate functions to produce one result row per group.
It sorts the result set in ascending order based on the specified columns.
It filters rows before any aggregation is performed.
It removes duplicate rows from the result set.
questions.distractor_a: It filters rows before any aggregation is performed.
questions.distractor_b: It removes duplicate rows from the result set.
questions.distractor_c: It sorts the result set in ascending order based on the specified columns.

questions.question: Which best describes the 'SELECT statement' as taught in the lecture?
options: It retrieves specified columns from a joined table, such as selecting a person's name and a thing's description after performing an inner join.
It only works with outer joins and cannot be used with inner joins.
It automatically deletes rows that do not match the join condition.
It creates a new table that permanently stores the joined data.
questions.distractor_a: It only works with outer joins and cannot be used with inner joins.
questions.distractor_b: It automatically deletes rows that do not match the join condition.
questions.distractor_c: It creates a new table that permanently stores the joined data.

questions.question: Which best describes the SQL JOIN as taught in the lecture?
options: A JOIN merges all rows from two tables regardless of any matching column.
A JOIN removes duplicate rows automatically from the result set.
A JOIN is used only for aggregating data across tables without selecting specific columns.
A JOIN combines rows from two tables based on a related column, producing a result set that includes columns from both tables.
questions.distractor_a: A JOIN is used only for aggregating data across tables without selecting specific columns.
questions.distractor_b: A JOIN removes duplicate rows automatically from the result set.
questions.distractor_c: A JOIN merges all rows from two tables regardless of any matching column.

questions.question: Which best describes 'SUM aggregation' as taught in the lecture?
options: It counts the number of rows in each group.
It averages the values in each group.
It sums the values of a column for each group defined by a GROUP BY clause.
It returns the maximum value in each group.
questions.distractor_a: It averages the values in each group.
questions.distractor_b: It returns the maximum value in each group.
questions.distractor_c: It counts the number of rows in each group.

questions.question: Which best describes 'auto‑generated ID' as taught in the lecture?
options: It can be manually set by the developer before the object is flushed.
It is assigned to a new object only after the session is flushed, allowing the object to receive an ID without immediately persisting it to the database.
It is assigned to an object only after it is permanently written to the database.
It is generated only when the transaction is committed, not during a flush.
questions.distractor_a: It is generated only when the transaction is committed, not during a flush.
questions.distractor_b: It is assigned to an object only after it is permanently written to the database.
questions.distractor_c: It can be manually set by the developer before the object is flushed.

questions.question: Which best describes the "auto‑increment primary key" as taught in the lecture?
options: It automatically assigns a unique, sequential numeric ID to each new row, and the next ID is always one greater than the current maximum, regardless of uncommitted changes.
It only works if the table has no existing rows.
It requires the user to manually provide the ID for each new row.
It resets to 1 every time the database is restarted.
questions.distractor_a: It only works if the table has no existing rows.
questions.distractor_b: It resets to 1 every time the database is restarted.
questions.distractor_c: It requires the user to manually provide the ID for each new row.

questions.question: Which best describes 'filter conditions' as taught in the lecture?
options: Filter conditions automatically delete rows that do not meet the specified criteria.
Filter conditions are applied by adding a WHERE clause to the SQL query string.
Filter conditions are only used for updating existing records, not for querying.
Filter conditions use the filter function to restrict query results based on a predicate, such as selecting only people whose age exceeds a given value.
questions.distractor_a: Filter conditions are only used for updating existing records, not for querying.
questions.distractor_b: Filter conditions are applied by adding a WHERE clause to the SQL query string.
questions.distractor_c: Filter conditions automatically delete rows that do not meet the specified criteria.

questions.question: Which best describes "selecting fields" as taught in the lecture?
options: When you query with session.query(Person.name, Person.age) you receive a list of tuples containing only the specified columns instead of full Person objects.
It automatically creates new database rows for each selected field.
It requires writing raw SQL join statements to retrieve the fields.
It returns a single dictionary with field names as keys and values as strings.
questions.distractor_a: It automatically creates new database rows for each selected field.
questions.distractor_b: It requires writing raw SQL join statements to retrieve the fields.
questions.distractor_c: It returns a single dictionary with field names as keys and values as strings.

questions.question: Which best describes 'session.flush' as taught in the lecture?
options: It only assigns temporary IDs without touching the database.
It permanently saves all changes to the database immediately.
It temporarily writes pending changes to the database to generate IDs, but does not commit them permanently.
It rolls back all pending changes and discards them from the session.
questions.distractor_a: It permanently saves all changes to the database immediately.
questions.distractor_b: It only assigns temporary IDs without touching the database.
questions.distractor_c: It rolls back all pending changes and discards them from the session.

questions.question: Which best describes 'session.query' as taught in the lecture?
options: It automatically creates new database tables when called.
It is used to retrieve Python objects from the database by specifying the target class or fields, returning a list of objects or values.
It requires manual SQL join statements to combine related tables.
It only works with primitive data types, not ORM classes.
questions.distractor_a: It automatically creates new database tables when called.
questions.distractor_b: It only works with primitive data types, not ORM classes.
questions.distractor_c: It requires manual SQL join statements to combine related tables.

questions.question: Which best describes 'transaction commit' as taught in the lecture?
options: It finalizes all pending changes, making them permanently visible in the database and allowing related IDs to be used in subsequent operations.
It assigns new IDs to all rows in the table regardless of whether they were inserted or updated.
It automatically rolls back any changes that were not explicitly deleted before the commit.
It only saves the current transaction’s data to memory but does not make it visible to other connections.
questions.distractor_a: It assigns new IDs to all rows in the table regardless of whether they were inserted or updated.
questions.distractor_b: It only saves the current transaction’s data to memory but does not make it visible to other connections.
questions.distractor_c: It automatically rolls back any changes that were not explicitly deleted before the commit.

questions.question: Which best describes 'tuple vs object results' as taught in the lecture?
options: The result is a dictionary mapping field names to values for each row.
The result is a single Python object, even when multiple rows are returned.
The result is always a list of tuples, regardless of whether objects or fields are selected.
When the query selects entire objects, the result is a list of Python objects; when it selects individual fields, the result is a list of tuples containing those field values.
questions.distractor_a: The result is always a list of tuples, regardless of whether objects or fields are selected.
questions.distractor_b: The result is a dictionary mapping field names to values for each row.
questions.distractor_c: The result is a single Python object, even when multiple rows are returned.

questions.question: Which best describes Flask‑SQLAlchemy as taught in the lecture?
options: Flask‑SQLAlchemy is a lightweight wrapper around SQLAlchemy that lets you use SQLAlchemy’s ORM features directly in a Flask application.
Flask‑SQLAlchemy requires you to write raw SQL queries instead of using ORM models.
Flask‑SQLAlchemy is only used for handling Flask session data, not database interactions.
Flask‑SQLAlchemy replaces SQLAlchemy entirely with a new query language specific to Flask.
questions.distractor_a: Flask‑SQLAlchemy is only used for handling Flask session data, not database interactions.
questions.distractor_b: Flask‑SQLAlchemy requires you to write raw SQL queries instead of using ORM models.
questions.distractor_c: Flask‑SQLAlchemy replaces SQLAlchemy entirely with a new query language specific to Flask.

questions.question: Which best describes the HAVING clause as taught in the lecture?
options: The HAVING clause replaces the WHERE clause in all SQL queries.
The HAVING clause is used to filter rows before any aggregation occurs.
The HAVING clause filters aggregated results after GROUP BY, allowing conditions on aggregate expressions such as SUM or AVG.
The HAVING clause can only compare aggregate values to constants, not to other columns.
questions.distractor_a: The HAVING clause is used to filter rows before any aggregation occurs.
questions.distractor_b: The HAVING clause replaces the WHERE clause in all SQL queries.
questions.distractor_c: The HAVING clause can only compare aggregate values to constants, not to other columns.

questions.question: Which best describes the use of 'HAVING' as taught in the lecture?
options: It replaces the WHERE clause for all types of conditions.
It is used to filter rows before any grouping occurs.
It filters grouped query results after aggregation, allowing conditions on aggregate values such as requiring a function's value to be above 50.
It is only applicable when no GROUP BY clause is present.
questions.distractor_a: It is used to filter rows before any grouping occurs.
questions.distractor_b: It replaces the WHERE clause for all types of conditions.
questions.distractor_c: It is only applicable when no GROUP BY clause is present.

questions.question: Which best describes 'pandas read_sql' as taught in the lecture?
options: It writes a pandas DataFrame directly into a SQL table without needing a query string.
It requires a separate SQLAlchemy session object instead of an engine to function.
It automatically creates a new database if one does not exist when called.
It loads the result of a SQL query into a pandas DataFrame by passing the query string and a database connection (engine).
questions.distractor_a: It requires a separate SQLAlchemy session object instead of an engine to function.
questions.distractor_b: It writes a pandas DataFrame directly into a SQL table without needing a query string.
questions.distractor_c: It automatically creates a new database if one does not exist when called.

questions.question: Which best describes 'INNER JOIN' as taught in the lecture?
options: It keeps all rows from both tables, even if there is no matching row in the other table, filling gaps with NULLs.
It returns all rows from the first table and matches from the second, filling missing values with NULLs.
It combines two tables and returns only rows where the join condition matches in both tables, excluding rows that have no match.
It merges tables based on any common column, regardless of the join condition specified.
questions.distractor_a: It keeps all rows from both tables, even if there is no matching row in the other table, filling gaps with NULLs.
questions.distractor_b: It returns all rows from the first table and matches from the second, filling missing values with NULLs.
questions.distractor_c: It merges tables based on any common column, regardless of the join condition specified.

questions.question: Which best describes the 'delete' operation as taught in the lecture?
options: Delete permanently erases the database schema along with the data.
Delete can only be applied to entire tables, not individual records.
Delete automatically rolls back if the session is closed before commit.
The delete function removes selected records from the database, and the changes are persisted only after calling session.commit().
questions.distractor_a: Delete permanently erases the database schema along with the data.
questions.distractor_b: Delete can only be applied to entire tables, not individual records.
questions.distractor_c: Delete automatically rolls back if the session is closed before commit.

questions.question: Which best describes the role of session.commit after delete/update as taught in the lecture?
options: The delete or update operation itself writes directly to the database, so session.commit has no effect on it.
session.commit is only needed when inserting new records, not when deleting or updating.
Calling session.commit after a delete or update is optional because the changes are automatically flushed to the database.
After issuing a delete or update query, session.commit must be called to persist the changes to the database; without it the operations remain in the session only and the database is unchanged.
questions.distractor_a: Calling session.commit after a delete or update is optional because the changes are automatically flushed to the database.
questions.distractor_b: The delete or update operation itself writes directly to the database, so session.commit has no effect on it.
questions.distractor_c: session.commit is only needed when inserting new records, not when deleting or updating.

questions.question: Which best describes the concept of 'filter' as taught in the lecture?
options: It narrows the set of returned objects by specifying criteria in a query, producing only those that match the conditions.
It removes duplicate objects from the result set regardless of query conditions.
It converts database rows into JSON strings before returning them.
It automatically sorts the returned objects by their primary key.
questions.distractor_a: It converts database rows into JSON strings before returning them.
questions.distractor_b: It removes duplicate objects from the result set regardless of query conditions.
questions.distractor_c: It automatically sorts the returned objects by their primary key.

questions.question: Which best describes a LEFT OUTER JOIN as taught in the lecture?
options: It returns only rows that have matches in both tables.
It returns all rows from the left table and matching rows from the right table, filling in NULLs when there is no match.
It returns all rows from the right table and matching rows from the left table, filling in NULLs when there is no match.
It returns only the rows that have no matches in the right table, showing NULLs for the right table columns.
questions.distractor_a: It returns only the rows that have no matches in the right table, showing NULLs for the right table columns.

questions.question: Which best describes the "update" operation as taught in the lecture?
options: It only modifies the in-memory Python objects without affecting the database.
It changes the values of existing database rows by specifying new values for selected columns, typically using a filter to target specific records.
It deletes rows that match a filter and then inserts new rows.
It creates new rows in the database with updated values.
questions.distractor_a: It creates new rows in the database with updated values.
questions.distractor_b: It only modifies the in-memory Python objects without affecting the database.
questions.distractor_c: It deletes rows that match a filter and then inserts new rows.

questions.question: Which best describes 'session.commit' as taught in the lecture?
options: It only logs the changes without affecting the database.
It automatically rolls back any uncommitted changes.
It writes all pending changes in the session to the database, finalizing the transaction.
It creates a new session object for database interaction.
questions.distractor_a: It only logs the changes without affecting the database.
questions.distractor_b: It automatically rolls back any uncommitted changes.
questions.distractor_c: It creates a new session object for database interaction.

questions.question: Which best describes "Querying with ORM" as taught in the lecture?
options: Querying with ORM eliminates the need for any database schema definitions in the code.
Querying with ORM allows you to use Python classes and methods like filter, order_by, and all to retrieve database records, with the ORM translating these calls into SQL behind the scenes.
Querying with ORM only works with Flask applications, not with Django or FastAPI.
Querying with ORM requires writing raw SQL queries in the code.
questions.distractor_a: Querying with ORM requires writing raw SQL queries in the code.
questions.distractor_b: Querying with ORM eliminates the need for any database schema definitions in the code.
questions.distractor_c: Querying with ORM only works with Flask applications, not with Django or FastAPI.

questions.question: Which best describes 'session.new' as taught in the lecture?
options: It automatically writes all changes to the database without needing a commit.
It creates a new database record immediately upon being called.
It is used to close an existing session and release resources.
It initializes a new session so that subsequent changes are tracked and can be committed to the database.
questions.distractor_a: It automatically writes all changes to the database without needing a commit.
questions.distractor_b: It creates a new database record immediately upon being called.
questions.distractor_c: It is used to close an existing session and release resources.

questions.question: Which best describes 'Session close/commit' as taught in the lecture?
options: Session.close() only rolls back uncommitted transactions and discards all changes made during the session.
Calling session.close() properly closes the database connection and automatically commits any pending changes that have not yet been committed.
Calling session.close() only terminates the connection but does not affect uncommitted changes.
Session.close() must be followed by session.commit() to persist changes; it does not commit automatically.
questions.distractor_a: Calling session.close() only terminates the connection but does not affect uncommitted changes.
questions.distractor_b: Session.close() must be followed by session.commit() to persist changes; it does not commit automatically.
questions.distractor_c: Session.close() only rolls back uncommitted transactions and discards all changes made during the session.
